title: Civil Engineering Basics
summary: An introduction to civil engineering: what civil engineers do, construction materials and estimating concrete, loads, stress and beams, soils and foundations, roads, drainage and water, and site safety and careers. All calculations were checked in code.
audience: School leavers, technicians, site workers and anyone interested in infrastructure

body.p: Civil engineering designs, builds and maintains the physical infrastructure that societies depend on: roads, bridges, railways, buildings, dams, water supply, sewers, ports and airports. It is one of the oldest branches of engineering and one of the most important for development, because good infrastructure lowers costs, connects markets and protects health.

list: Structural engineering: buildings, bridges and towers that safely carry loads.
Geotechnical engineering: soils, rock and foundations.
Transportation engineering: roads, railways, traffic and airports.
Water resources and hydraulics: dams, canals, flood control and irrigation.
Environmental and public health engineering: water treatment, sanitation and waste.
Construction management: planning, cost, quality and safety on site.

body.p: A typical project moves through identifying a need, feasibility studies, site investigation, design, tendering and procurement, construction, handover, and operation and maintenance. Maintenance is often neglected, yet a road that is not maintained can fail in a few years and cost far more to rebuild than to repair.

body.tip: Professional engineers register with a national body, such as ECSA in South Africa, COREN in Nigeria or the Engineers Board of Kenya, and follow codes of practice.

list: Concrete: cement, sand, stone (aggregate) and water. Strong in compression, weak in tension.
Reinforced concrete: steel bars carry the tension, so beams and slabs can span distances.
Steel: strong in tension and compression, used for frames, bridges and roofs; must be protected from rust.
Masonry: bricks and blocks bonded with mortar, good in compression for walls.
Timber: light, renewable and easy to work, but must be protected from rot and termites.
Bitumen and aggregates for road surfaces.

body.p: A slab 5 m long, 4 m wide and 0.15 m thick needs 5 x 4 x 0.15 = 3 m³ of concrete. Because dry materials shrink when mixed with water, engineers multiply by about 1.54 to get the dry volume: 4.62 m³. In a 1 : 2 : 4 mix (cement : sand : stone), cement is 1 part in 7, so 4.62 / 7 = 0.66 m³. At about 1440 kg/m³, that is about 950 kg, or 19 bags of 50 kg.
Water-cement ratio strongly affects strength: adding extra water makes concrete easier to place but weaker. Concrete must also be cured, kept moist for several days, to gain strength.

body.tip: Always add a margin for waste, typically 5 to 10%, when ordering materials.

body.p: Structures must carry loads safely to the ground. Dead loads are the weight of the structure itself; live loads come from people, furniture, vehicles and stored goods; environmental loads include wind, earthquakes, water and temperature changes.

Stress is force divided by area. A column 0.2 m x 0.2 m carrying 100 kN has a stress of 100 000 N / 0.04 m² = 2 500 000 Pa, or 2.5 MPa. Engineers compare this with the strength of the material and apply safety factors.

list: A beam carrying a load bends: the top is squeezed (compression) and the bottom is stretched (tension).
For a simply supported beam with a uniform load w over span L, the largest bending moment is wL²/8. For w = 10 kN/m and L = 6 m, that is 10 x 36 / 8 = 45 kNm.
For a single point load P at mid-span, the maximum moment is PL/4: 20 kN on a 6 m span gives 30 kNm.
Doubling the span quadruples the moment under a uniform load, which is why long spans need deeper beams.

body.tip: Trace the load path: from slab to beam to column to foundation to soil. Every link must be strong enough.

body.p: Every structure rests on soil or rock, so understanding the ground is essential. Site investigation uses trial pits, boreholes and laboratory tests to find soil types, strength, groundwater levels and problems such as expansive clays, which swell when wet and shrink when dry and can crack buildings.

The safe bearing capacity is the pressure the soil can carry without failing or settling too much. A column load of 200 kN on soil with a safe bearing capacity of 100 kPa (100 kN/m²) needs a footing area of 200 / 100 = 2 m², for example a square footing of 1.5 m x 1.5 m (2.25 m², rounded up for a margin).

list: Strip footings support walls.
Pad footings support individual columns.
Raft foundations spread the load of the whole building over weak soil.
Piles carry loads down to stronger layers deep below.

body.p: Drainage matters: water softens soils and causes most foundation and road failures.

body.tip: Never skip site investigation to save money; foundation failures are among the most expensive to fix.

body.p: A road is built in layers: the natural ground (subgrade), compacted sub-base and base layers of gravel or crushed stone, and a surface of asphalt, surface seal or concrete. Gradient is rise over run: a road rising 3 m over 150 m has a gradient of 2%. Roads are shaped with a camber so rain runs off to side drains.

Flow in a pipe is area times velocity: Q = A x v. A 300 mm pipe has an area of about 0.0707 m²; at 1.5 m/s it carries about 0.106 m³/s, or 106 litres per second. Culverts carry streams under roads, and must be sized for heavy storms, which are becoming more intense with climate change.

list: Water supply: source, treatment, storage (reservoirs and tanks) and distribution pipes.
Sanitation: sewers, treatment works, or on-site systems such as septic tanks and improved pit latrines.
Leaks and illegal connections cause large non-revenue water losses in many cities.

body.tip: Most road damage starts with water. Keep drains clear and seal cracks early.

body.p: Construction sites are hazardous. Leading causes of injury and death include falls from height, collapsing excavations, being struck by vehicles or falling objects, and electrocution.

list: Wear personal protective equipment: hard hat, safety boots, high-visibility vest, gloves and eye protection.
Support or slope trenches deeper than about 1.5 m.
Use guardrails, harnesses and properly erected scaffolding when working at height.
Keep the site tidy and plan vehicle routes.
Hold toolbox talks and report near misses.

body.p: Quality control includes testing concrete cubes, checking compaction and inspecting reinforcement before pouring. Sustainable design uses local materials, designs for climate resilience and maintenance, and considers the people affected, through environmental and social impact assessments.

Paths include engineering degrees, diplomas for technicians and technologists, and trades training. Roles range from design office work to site engineering, materials testing, project management and public works departments.

body.tip: Keep a site diary: dates, weather, work done, deliveries and instructions. It protects you in disputes.
